title: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)
summary: A scene represented as a continuous volumetric field of density and view-dependent colour, optimised from posed photographs by differentiable volume rendering.
context: Building on neural scene representations and classical volume rendering, NeRF (ECCV 2020) achieved photorealistic novel-view synthesis of complex real scenes. Camera poses came from COLMAP.
contribution: Positional encoding of coordinates, a view-dependent radiance MLP and hierarchical ray sampling made coordinate networks capture fine detail and non-Lambertian appearance.
technicalExplanation: F_θ: (x, d) → (σ, c). Pixel colour C(r) = Σᵢ Tᵢ (1 − exp(−σᵢδᵢ)) cᵢ along samples of ray r; θ is optimised to minimise photometric error over all training rays. Geometry is implicit in σ.
historicalSignificance: Changed the objective of reconstruction from explicit geometry to image reproduction, triggering thousands of follow-up works. Its relationship to photogrammetry is indirect: it depends on photogrammetric camera models and SfM poses but is evaluated by rendering metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) rather than geometric accuracy.
limitations: Hours of training per scene, slow rendering, static scenes only, sensitivity to pose errors, geometry not guaranteed to be accurate.

dates.improvements: NeRF in the Wild (2021), Mip-NeRF, Instant-NGP, Zip-NeRF

title: Neural implicit surfaces (NeuS, VolSDF)
summary: Volume rendering of signed distance functions to recover accurate surfaces rather than only appearance.
context: NeuS and VolSDF (NeurIPS 2021) reformulated density as a function of an SDF, making the zero level set a well-defined surface. Neuralangelo (CVPR 2023) scaled this to large scenes with hash grids.
contribution: Reconciled radiance-field optimisation with geometric surface reconstruction.
technicalExplanation: Density is derived from the SDF value through a logistic (NeuS) or Laplace CDF (VolSDF) so that rendering weights peak at the surface; an Eikonal loss regularises ‖∇f‖ = 1. Meshes are extracted by marching cubes.
historicalSignificance: Brought neural rendering back toward the measurement goals of photogrammetry, enabling comparisons on geometric benchmarks (e.g. DTU, Tanks and Temples).
limitations: Slow; watertight bias; thin structures difficult.

dates.improvements: 2D Gaussian Splatting (2024) offers faster surface reconstruction

title: Mip-NeRF, Mip-NeRF 360 and Zip-NeRF
summary: Anti-aliased radiance fields that reason about pixel footprints as cones, then extended to unbounded 360° scenes.
context: Mip-NeRF (ICCV 2021) addressed aliasing when views are at different scales; Mip-NeRF 360 (CVPR 2022) handled unbounded scenes with scene contraction and distortion regularisation; Zip-NeRF (ICCV 2023) combined anti-aliasing with grid-based speed.
contribution: Integrated positional encoding over conical frustums, and introduced the standard Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark scenes.
technicalExplanation: Each pixel's cone is approximated by Gaussians; the expected positional encoding attenuates frequencies larger than the footprint — a learned analogue of mipmapping.
historicalSignificance: Defined the quality ceiling and benchmark that 3D Gaussian Splatting was compared against.
limitations: Training and rendering remained slow compared with rasterisation.

title: Plenoxels and explicit radiance grids
summary: Radiance fields without neural networks: sparse voxel grids storing density and spherical-harmonic colour, optimised directly.
context: Plenoxels (CVPR 2022) and DVGO (CVPR 2022) showed that much of NeRF's quality comes from differentiable volume rendering, not the MLP. TensoRF (ECCV 2022) factorised grids into low-rank tensors.
contribution: Orders-of-magnitude faster optimisation; spherical harmonics as view-dependent colour model — later adopted by 3DGS.
technicalExplanation: Each voxel stores σ and SH coefficients; trilinear interpolation gives values along rays; total-variation regularisation; coarse-to-fine pruning.
historicalSignificance: Pointed toward explicit, primitive-based radiance representations — the conceptual step to Gaussian splatting.
limitations: Memory-heavy at high resolution.

title: Instant-NGP: multiresolution hash encoding
summary: A trainable multiresolution hash table of features plus a tiny MLP reduced NeRF training from hours to seconds–minutes.
context: Published in ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH 2022), with a fully fused CUDA implementation.
contribution: A compact, adaptive input encoding that made neural graphics primitives practical and interactive.
technicalExplanation: At L resolutions, a point's surrounding grid vertices are hashed into tables of learnable feature vectors; interpolated features from all levels are concatenated and decoded by a small MLP. Hash collisions are resolved implicitly by gradient averaging.
historicalSignificance: Made radiance fields usable in practice and spread them beyond research labs; its encoding became a standard component (e.g. Nerfstudio's nerfacto, Zip-NeRF, Neuralangelo).
limitations: Rendering still ray-marched; quality below Mip-NeRF 360 on unbounded scenes.

title: 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: A scene represented by millions of anisotropic 3D Gaussians, optimised from photographs and rendered in real time by differentiable rasterisation.
context: Published in ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH 2023), it matched or exceeded Mip-NeRF 360 quality while rendering at real-time rates (≥30 fps at 1080p) and training in tens of minutes.
contribution: Combined SfM point initialisation, EWA splatting, spherical-harmonic colour and a fast tile-based differentiable rasteriser with adaptive density control (clone, split, prune).
technicalExplanation: Each Gaussian has mean μ, covariance Σ = R S Sᵀ Rᵀ (rotation quaternion and scale), opacity α and SH colour. Gaussians are projected (Σ′ = J W Σ Wᵀ Jᵀ), depth-sorted per tile and alpha-blended: C = Σᵢ cᵢ αᵢ Πⱼ<ᵢ (1 − αⱼ). Gradients flow to all parameters.
historicalSignificance: Returned to explicit, point-like primitives — conceptually closer to photogrammetric point clouds — while retaining radiance-field optimisation. It rapidly became the dominant representation for novel-view synthesis, dynamic reconstruction and real-time spatial applications.
limitations: Large memory footprint; popping and aliasing; Gaussians are not a well-defined surface; dependent on SfM initialisation; floaters in poorly observed areas.

dates.adoption: Very rapid adoption 2023–2024, including commercial viewers and capture apps

title: Anti-aliased and surface-aligned Gaussians
summary: Refinements making Gaussian splatting robust across scales and capable of accurate surface reconstruction.
context: Mip-Splatting (CVPR 2024) added 3D smoothing and 2D mip filters; SuGaR (CVPR 2024) aligned Gaussians to surfaces for mesh extraction; 2D Gaussian Splatting (SIGGRAPH 2024) replaced 3D ellipsoids with oriented surfels.
contribution: Addressed two weaknesses of 3DGS relevant to metric use: scale-dependent artefacts and ill-defined geometry.
technicalExplanation: 2DGS represents each primitive as a planar disk with explicit normal, computing exact ray–splat intersections; depth-distortion and normal-consistency losses yield view-consistent geometry.
historicalSignificance: Signals a recurring theme: once appearance is solved, the field returns to geometric accuracy — photogrammetry's original goal.
limitations: Trade-offs between rendering quality and geometric fidelity remain.

title: Hierarchical and scalable Gaussian representations
summary: Level-of-detail hierarchies and chunked training to reconstruct and render very large scenes.
context: Hierarchical 3D Gaussians (ACM TOG, SIGGRAPH 2024) trained kilometre-scale captures in chunks and merged them into a LOD tree. Parallel work addressed compression and streaming; open libraries such as gsplat standardised implementations.
contribution: Made Gaussian splatting viable at city/street scale with bounded rendering cost.
technicalExplanation: Gaussians are merged bottom-up into parent Gaussians; a cut through the tree selects primitives by projected size; chunks are trained independently and consolidated.
historicalSignificance: Brings Gaussian representations toward the scales historically served by aerial photogrammetry and mobile mapping.
limitations: Large storage; consistent appearance across chunks; georeferencing and accuracy not part of the formulation.

title: Gaussian Splatting SLAM
summary: Tracking and mapping with a Gaussian scene representation, producing photorealistic maps online.
context: SplaTAM (RGB-D) and Gaussian Splatting SLAM / MonoGS (monocular and RGB-D), both CVPR 2024, replaced sparse maps and TSDFs with Gaussians optimised incrementally.
contribution: Unified the SLAM lineage with the radiance-field lineage: the map is simultaneously a localisation structure and a renderable scene.
technicalExplanation: Camera pose is optimised by photometric (and depth) rendering loss against the current Gaussian map; new Gaussians are added where silhouettes indicate unexplored space; keyframe windows are jointly refined.
historicalSignificance: A step toward persistent, real-time spatial representations for robotics and mixed reality.
limitations: Speed and scale behind classical SLAM; dynamic content; drift without loop closure.

title: Deformable NeRFs: D-NeRF and Nerfies
summary: Dynamic scenes modelled as a canonical radiance field plus a time- or frame-conditioned deformation field.
context: D-NeRF (CVPR 2021) introduced a time-conditioned deformation network on synthetic monocular sequences; Nerfies (ICCV 2021) reconstructed casually captured deforming subjects with per-frame latent codes and elastic regularisation.
contribution: Established the canonical-space-plus-deformation paradigm for 4D neural reconstruction.
technicalExplanation: Ψ(x, t) → Δx maps a point at time t into canonical space, where a static NeRF is queried. Regularisers (elastic, smoothness) constrain the ill-posed motion.
historicalSignificance: Opened dynamic reconstruction to neural methods; the same decomposition reappears in deformable 3D Gaussians.
limitations: Topology changes; large motions; monocular ambiguity; many benchmark sequences contain unrealistic camera motion ('teleportation').

title: HyperNeRF
summary: Topologically varying scenes modelled as slices through a higher-dimensional radiance field.
context: Published in ACM TOG (SIGGRAPH Asia 2021), HyperNeRF addressed topology changes (e.g. a mouth opening) that continuous deformation fields cannot represent.
contribution: Ambient ('hyper-space') dimensions inspired by level-set methods let the canonical template vary.
technicalExplanation: Each frame is a learned slice (x′, w(x,t)) through a field defined over 3D + ambient coordinates; deformation still maps x to x′.
historicalSignificance: Clarified that 4D reconstruction is not merely 3D plus motion: representation topology itself may change over time.
limitations: Monocular ambiguity; slow optimisation.

title: Space-time radiance fields for video
summary: Radiance fields conditioned directly on time, with scene flow or factorised space-time grids.
context: Neural Scene Flow Fields (CVPR 2021) modelled 3D scene flow from monocular video; DyNeRF / Neural 3D Video Synthesis (CVPR 2022) captured multi-view video with a time-conditioned field; K-Planes and HexPlane (CVPR 2023) factorised 4D into planes for speed.
contribution: Introduced explicit time-conditioned (rather than canonical-deformation) representations and multi-view video benchmarks.
technicalExplanation: K-Planes represents a 4D field with six planes (xy, xz, yz, xt, yt, zt); features are multiplied and decoded. Scene-flow fields enforce temporal consistency between neighbouring times.
historicalSignificance: The multi-view video datasets (e.g. DyNeRF's Neural 3D Video) became standard benchmarks for 4D Gaussian methods.
limitations: Training cost; temporal flicker; memory.

title: Dynamic 3D Gaussians
summary: Persistent Gaussians tracked through time in multi-view video, yielding dense 6-DOF tracking as a by-product of reconstruction.
context: Published at 3DV 2024 (arXiv August 2023), using the CMU Panoptic Studio sequences.
contribution: Treated each Gaussian as a physical particle with a trajectory; local rigidity and isometry priors make motion consistent.
technicalExplanation: Gaussians keep colour, opacity and size fixed; positions and rotations are optimised per timestep, initialised from the previous frame, with physically motivated regularisers over neighbours.
historicalSignificance: Connected reconstruction and tracking: correspondences across time emerge from the representation itself — a 4D analogue of tie points.
limitations: Requires dense synchronised multi-view capture; struggles with newly appearing content.

title: 4D-GS and deformable Gaussians
institutions: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
summary: A canonical set of 3D Gaussians deformed over time by a learned field, enabling real-time dynamic rendering.
context: 4D-GS (Wu et al., CVPR 2024) used a HexPlane-encoded deformation network; Deformable 3D Gaussians (Yang et al., CVPR 2024) used an MLP deformation field. Both carried the D-NeRF paradigm over to splatting.
contribution: Real-time rendering of dynamic scenes with compact storage, by predicting per-Gaussian position, rotation and scale offsets.
technicalExplanation: For time t, a spatial–temporal encoder (multi-resolution planes) produces features for each canonical Gaussian; small heads decode Δμ, Δr, Δs; the deformed set is rasterised as in 3DGS.
historicalSignificance: Became a standard baseline for dynamic Gaussian research and practical volumetric video.
limitations: Canonical assumption struggles with appearing/disappearing content and large motion; deformation fields may not reflect physical motion.
uncertainty: The name '4D Gaussian Splatting' is used by several distinct papers; check authors when citing.

title: Native 4D and spacetime Gaussians
summary: Gaussians defined directly in 4D space-time, sliced at each time to obtain 3D Gaussians.
context: Yang et al. (ICLR 2024) proposed 4D Gaussian primitives with 4D rotations and 4D spherindrical harmonics; Spacetime Gaussians (Li et al., CVPR 2024) added temporal opacity and polynomial motion.
contribution: Treated time as a coordinate of the primitive rather than as a deformation of a canonical scene, naturally handling transient content.
technicalExplanation: A 4D Gaussian N(μ₄, Σ₄) conditioned on t gives a 3D Gaussian with time-dependent mean and covariance, plus a marginal temporal weight that fades it in and out.
historicalSignificance: Makes the 4D representation explicit — the conceptual endpoint of moving from static photogrammetric points to space-time primitives.
limitations: Memory grows with temporal extent; correspondence over time is not guaranteed.

title: Monocular 4D reconstruction with priors
summary: Dynamic reconstruction from a single casual video by combining Gaussians with learned depth, tracking and segmentation priors.
context: Shape of Motion (2024) represented motion with a compact set of SE(3) motion bases and supervised it with off-the-shelf monocular depth and 2D long-range tracks.
contribution: Demonstrated that 4D reconstruction from everyday video is possible when geometry is regularised by foundation-model priors.
technicalExplanation: Each Gaussian's trajectory is a weighted combination of a few shared rigid motion bases; losses on rendered depth, 2D tracks and masks constrain the ill-posed problem.
historicalSignificance: Shifts the evidence for geometry from parallax alone to parallax plus learned priors — a significant epistemological change relative to photogrammetry.
limitations: Dependence on prior quality; difficult to separate prior-induced from observed structure.
uncertainty: Rapidly evolving; venues and successor methods may change the picture.

title: DUSt3R
summary: A transformer that regresses dense 3D pointmaps for an image pair directly, without known intrinsics or poses.
context: Published at CVPR 2024 (arXiv December 2023), DUSt3R reframed two-view reconstruction as direct regression of 3D points in a common frame.
contribution: Replaced the classical chain (features → matching → essential matrix → triangulation) by one network; cameras are recovered from the pointmaps afterwards.
technicalExplanation: Two images are encoded by a shared ViT; decoders with cross-attention output, for each pixel, a 3D point in the first camera's frame plus confidence. Multiple pairs are aligned by a global optimisation over pointmaps.
historicalSignificance: Inverts the historical order of photogrammetry: geometry is predicted first and camera parameters derived from it.
limitations: Pairwise; quadratic global alignment; accuracy below optimisation-based SfM on well-textured data; trained on specific datasets.

dates.adoption: Rapidly adopted as initialisation for sparse-view NeRF/3DGS

title: MASt3R
summary: DUSt3R extended with dense local features for metric pointmaps and accurate matching.
context: Published at ECCV 2024; follow-ups (MASt3R-SfM) built full SfM pipelines on its matches.
contribution: Grounded pointmap regression in explicit correspondence, improving precision and enabling use inside classical pipelines.
technicalExplanation: A second head outputs dense descriptors trained with a matching loss; fast reciprocal matching extracts correspondences that can feed bundle adjustment.
historicalSignificance: An example of hybridisation: learned inference supplies correspondences and initialisation, classical optimisation supplies rigour.
limitations: Still pair-based at its core.

title: Feed-forward Gaussian and large reconstruction models
summary: Networks that output a renderable 3D representation (Gaussians or triplanes) from a few images in a single forward pass.
context: LRM (ICLR 2024) predicted triplane NeRFs of objects from a single image; pixelSplat (CVPR 2024) and MVSplat (ECCV 2024) predicted per-pixel Gaussians from image pairs.
contribution: Amortised per-scene optimisation into a learned model, generalising across scenes.
technicalExplanation: Image features (with epipolar or cost-volume attention) predict, for each pixel, a depth distribution and Gaussian parameters; the result is rendered with the 3DGS rasteriser and trained on novel-view losses across datasets.
historicalSignificance: Moves 3D representation toward a generic learned function of images, blurring reconstruction and generation.
limitations: Limited to few views and bounded scenes; generalisation; fidelity below per-scene optimisation.

title: MonST3R and CUT3R: dynamic and persistent pointmaps
summary: Pointmap regression extended to dynamic scenes (MonST3R) and to a recurrent model with a persistent scene state (CUT3R).
context: MonST3R (ICLR 2025) fine-tuned DUSt3R to estimate geometry per timestep in dynamic videos. CUT3R (CVPR 2025) processes image streams continuously, updating a learned state that accumulates scene knowledge.
contribution: Brought feed-forward geometry to time-varying scenes and introduced a learned, persistent 'memory' of the scene.
technicalExplanation: CUT3R: each new image interacts with a state token set via a transformer; the model outputs a pointmap in a world frame and updates the state; the state can also be queried from unseen viewpoints.
historicalSignificance: Links feed-forward reconstruction to SLAM and to persistent spatial representations.
limitations: Drift over long sequences; accuracy and calibration still under evaluation.
uncertainty: Emerging research; long-term significance not yet established.

title: Fast3R
summary: Pointmap regression for many views in one forward pass, scaling beyond pairs.
context: Published at CVPR 2025; processes hundreds to over a thousand images jointly with all-to-all attention.
contribution: Removed DUSt3R's pairwise processing and global alignment, improving speed and scalability.
technicalExplanation: All images are tokenised and fused by a single transformer with image-index embeddings; heads predict global and local pointmaps with confidence.
historicalSignificance: Part of the 2025 shift from pairwise to multi-view feed-forward reconstruction.
limitations: Memory scaling of attention; accuracy relative to SfM on large scenes.

title: VGGT — Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer
institutions: Visual Geometry Group, University of Oxford
summary: A large feed-forward transformer predicting camera parameters, depth maps, pointmaps and tracks for one to hundreds of views in about a second.
context: Published at CVPR 2025, where it received the Best Paper award. It is trained on a broad mixture of 3D-annotated datasets.
contribution: Predicts the full set of quantities classically produced by an SfM + MVS pipeline, directly; its outputs can be refined with bundle adjustment and used to initialise 3DGS.
technicalExplanation: DINO-patchified images are processed by alternating frame-wise and global self-attention; camera tokens yield intrinsics and extrinsics; dense heads predict depth, pointmaps and tracking features.
historicalSignificance: The clearest instance of a '3D foundation model' for geometry: it competes with — and can initialise — optimisation-based pipelines descended from bundle adjustment.
limitations: Training-data dependence; evaluation of metric accuracy and failure modes is ongoing.
uncertainty: Emerging research; long-term significance not yet established.

title: Physics-integrated Gaussians
summary: Reconstructed Gaussians used directly as particles in a continuum-mechanics simulation.
context: PhysGaussian (CVPR 2024) coupled 3DGS with the material point method to generate physically plausible motion of reconstructed objects.
contribution: A unified representation for rendering and simulation — 'what you see is what you simulate'.
technicalExplanation: Gaussians carry material properties; MPM evolves their positions and deformation gradients, which also deform their covariances for rendering.
historicalSignificance: Extends reconstruction from describing a scene to predicting its behaviour, a step toward physically grounded world representations.
limitations: Material parameters are assigned, not measured; interior is not observed.

title: Spatial foundation models and persistent scene representations
summary: Large models and representations that unify geometry, appearance and semantics, and persist and update over time.
context: Several strands converge: general depth models (e.g. Depth Anything, CVPR 2024), feed-forward geometry (VGGT, CUT3R), language-embedded radiance fields (LERF, ICCV 2023) and Gaussian SLAM. Together they suggest 'spatial intelligence' systems that maintain a persistent, queryable model of the environment.
contribution: Not a single method but a research programme: reconstruction as one capability of general spatial perception models.
technicalExplanation: Common ingredients: ViT backbones pretrained on large image corpora; heads for depth, pose, points and semantics; explicit (Gaussian) or latent scene states updated online; language features distilled into 3D.
historicalSignificance: If successful, it would relocate reconstruction from per-project measurement to always-on infrastructure — raising the same questions of accuracy, reliability and versioning that photogrammetry and geodesy addressed for maps.
limitations: Definitions are unsettled; evaluation of metric reliability is limited; claims evolve quickly.
uncertainty: This is an emerging, loosely defined direction rather than a settled milestone.

title: World models
summary: Learned models that predict how an environment evolves in response to actions, increasingly generating explorable 3D-consistent scenes.
context: Ha and Schmidhuber's 'World Models' (2018) learned compressed environment dynamics for control. Generative interactive environments (Genie, ICML 2024) and world foundation models for physical AI (NVIDIA Cosmos, 2025) extend this toward video-based simulators.
contribution: Shifts the target from reconstructing what was observed to predicting what could be observed — a generative rather than metrological relation to the world.
technicalExplanation: Typically a latent encoder, a dynamics model (often a transformer or diffusion model) conditioned on actions, and a decoder to video frames; 3D consistency may be implicit rather than enforced by geometry.
historicalSignificance: Related to, but distinct from, image-based reconstruction. Reconstructed scenes increasingly serve as training data, priors or evaluation for world models, and world models as priors for reconstruction.
limitations: Geometric consistency and physical correctness are not guaranteed; not a measurement method.

dates.invention: Concept in control theory and RL predates 2018

uncertainty: Emerging and partly industrial; claims are hard to verify independently. Included to situate reconstruction within a broader landscape, not as a photogrammetric milestone.
